sections.name: PARTIES
sentences: Plaintiff, Olga Nowak, is an adult individual residing at 3300 Neshaminy Boulevard, Apt. 589, Bensalem, PA 19020.
Plaintiff is female.
Defendant, Thoroughbred Services, Inc., is a corporation or other entity that maintains a principal place of business and/or registered office at 3001 Street Road, Bensalem, PA 19020.

sections.name: JURISDICTION
sentences: This is a civil action arising under the laws of the United States and is brought pursuant to the Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, as amended, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e et seq. (“Title VII”); and, 42 U.S.C. §1981a.
This Court also has jurisdiction of the claims pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1331 and 28 U.S.C. §1343.
This Court also has pendent and supplemental jurisdiction over plaintiff’s state law claims pursuant to 28 U.S.C. §1367.
This is a civil action arising under the laws of the United States and is brought pursuant to the Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, as amended, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e et seq.

sections.name: VENUE
sentences: Defendant transacts business and is found in this district.

sections.name: FACTUAL BACKGROUND
sentences: Nowak began employment with defendant in or about January 2016 as a Safety Coordinator reporting to Samuel Elliott (male).
Nowak was a licensed racing official with extensive experience as a thoroughbred trainer, jockey and exercise rider.
One of Nowak’s duties was reporting safety violations.
Elliott left defendant in or about April 2018.
In or about October 2018 Nowak began reporting to David Osojnak (male) who was hired in or about October 2018.
In or about November 2018 Nowak informed Osojnak of her intention to obtain a Safety Steward accreditation.
Osojnak was supportive and even told Nowak that he would try to get defendant to pay for the course Nowak needed to attend to obtain the accreditation.
Also in or about November 2018, Osojnak instructed Nowak to stop reporting certain individuals for safety violations, despite state law that required Nowak to report such violations.
Despite the instruction, Nowak continued to report the safety violations as she was the Safety Coordinator and required by state law to report the violations.
Nowak was discharged on or about February 27, 2019.
Osojnak told Nowak that she was being discharged because she didn’t have the skills to perform the Safety Coordinator position.

This, despite the fact that Nowak had been performing the position for more than three years and despite the fact that Osojnak had previously indicated his support for Nowak obtaining a Safety Steward accreditation.
Nowak was replaced by Donnie Smith (male) who had been working in the office.
Nowak contends that she had as much, or more, experience than Smith as a thoroughbred jockey, exercise rider and/or trainer; and was as, or more, qualified than Smith for the position.

At all times material hereto defendant was acting by and through its duly appointed employees, agents, servants and/or workmen who were acting within the course and scope of said agency and/or employment relationship with the express and/or implied permission of the defendant.
Nowak received a “Right to Sue” letter on or about March 10, 2020. (See, letter from EEOC dated March 10, 2020 attached hereto as Exhibit “A.”).

sections.name: COUNT - I
sentences: PLAINTIFF v. DEFENDANT.
Defendant’s conduct, as outlined above, including, but not limited to, discharging plaintiff constitutes unlawful gender discrimination in violation of Title VII.
As a direct result of defendant’s unlawful and wrongful conduct, plaintiff has suffered substantial economic harm including, inter alia, lost wages and benefits.

sections.name: COUNT - II
sentences: PLAINTIFF v. DEFENDANT.
Defendant’s conduct, as outlined above, including, but not limited to, discharging plaintiff constitutes unlawful gender discrimination in violation of the PHRA.
As a direct result of defendant’s unlawful and wrongful conduct, plaintiff has suffered substantial economic harm including, inter alia, lost wages and benefits.

sections.name: COUNT - III
sentences: PLAINTIFF v. DEFENDANT.

Defendant’s conduct in discharging Nowak after she reported certain safety violations that she was instructed not to report constitutes wrongful discharge in violation of an express public policy of the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania.
As a direct result of defendant’s unlawful and wrongful conduct, Nowak has suffered substantial economic harm including, inter alia, lost wages and benefits.

sections.name: PRAYER FOR RELIEF
sentences: WHEREFORE, plaintiff seeks damages to the extent that she has been harmed by defendant’s unlawful conduct and specifically prays that the Court grant the following relief: Enter an Order compelling defendant to reinstate plaintiff to her former position with all accrued seniority and benefits so as to put plaintiff in the same position as though she was never discharged; Award to plaintiff back salary, wages, fringe benefits, front pay, and other allowable damages, together with prejudgment interest pursuant to the Title VII, the PHRA and common law; Award to plaintiff compensatory damages pursuant to the Title VII, the PHRA and common law; Award to plaintiff punitive damages pursuant to the Title VII and common law; Award to plaintiff and her counsel attorney's fees, costs and disbursements pursuant to Title VII and the PHRA; and, Any other equitable or legal relief that this Court deems appropriate.
Plaintiff seeks damages to the extent that she has been harmed by defendant’s unlawful conduct and specifically prays that the Court grant the following relief:.

Enter an Order compelling defendant to reinstate plaintiff to her former position with all accrued seniority and benefits so as to put plaintiff in the same position as though she was never discharged.

sections.name: PLAINTIFF’S CLAIMS UNDER TITLE VII
sentences: Plaintiff hereby incorporates by reference all of the allegations contained in paragraphs 1 through 21 inclusive as fully as though the same were herein set forth at length.

Defendant’s conduct, as outlined above, including, but not limited to, discharging plaintiff constitutes unlawful gender discrimination in violation of Title VII. As a direct result of defendant’s unlawful and wrongful conduct, plaintiff has suffered substantial economic harm including, inter alia, lost wages and benefits.
In addition, defendant’s discriminatory conduct has caused plaintiff significant emotional distress.
Further, said discrimination was willful, intentional, outrageous, and/or in flagrant disregard of the provisions of Title VII thereby entitling plaintiff to punitive damages.

sections.name: PLAINTIFF’S CLAIMS UNDER THE PHRA
sentences: Plaintiff hereby incorporates by reference all of the allegations contained in paragraphs 1 through 26 inclusive as fully as though the same were herein set forth at length.
Defendant’s conduct, as outlined above, including, but not limited to, discharging plaintiff constitutes unlawful gender discrimination in violation of the PHRA.
As a direct result of defendant’s unlawful and wrongful conduct, plaintiff has suffered substantial economic harm including, inter alia, lost wages and benefits.
In addition, defendant’s discriminatory conduct has caused plaintiff significant emotional distress.

sections.name: PLAINTIFF’S COMMON LAW CLAIMS
sentences: Plaintiff hereby incorporates by reference all of the allegations contained in paragraphs 1 through 30 inclusive as fully as though the same were herein set forth at length.

At all times material hereto, 58 Pa. Code §163 et seq, set forth the Rules of Racing and was/is an expression of the public policy of the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania on the matters contained therein.
At all times material hereto, 58 Pa. Code §163.6 required racetrack officials, like Nowak, to report violations of the Rules of Racing.
At all times material hereto, 58 Pa. Code §163.291 addressed safety issues for the protection of patrons and racing personnel.
As a result, the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania determined that reporting safety violations is necessary to protect the health and welfare of racing personnel and patrons of a racetrack.

Defendant’s conduct in discharging Nowak after she reported certain safety violations that she was instructed not to report constitutes wrongful discharge in violation of an express public policy of the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania.
As a direct result of defendant’s unlawful and wrongful conduct, Nowak has suffered substantial economic harm including, inter alia, lost wages and benefits.
In addition, defendant’s conduct has caused Nowak significant emotional distress.
Further, said conduct was willful, intentional and/or outrageous, entitling Nowak to an award of punitive damages.
